summary: Comments from UCLA-CCN to the author of RFC 226 on her proposed host names. They support having standard names but object to the list, suggesting NIC site codes as a better base, questioning the length limit, and noting the list covers fewer hosts than were then on the network.

plainLanguage.summary: UCLA-CCN agrees that hosts should have standard names, but objects to the list proposed in RFC 226. It offers alternative naming sources and specific changes to the names for several hosts.

questions: what did ucla cc suggest about rfc 226
subtitle: UCLA-CCN's critique of the host mnemonic proposal in RFC 226.

tldr.problem: UCLA-CCN supported standard host mnemonics but considered the proposed list incomplete and some names poorly chosen.
tldr.mechanism: The comments suggest using NIC site codes, question a six-character limit and identify omissions and preferred names.
tldr.outcome: The RFC records a contribution to the discussion of host naming, without setting a final standard.

sections.title: Agreement and Main Concerns
sections.content:
UCLA-CCN agrees that a standard set of host mnemonics should be selected. It says the proposed set appears to reflect historical choices by TENEX Telnet programmers rather than a deliberate naming process.

The authors suggest that NIC site codes might be a better source because they had been selected with more care and were expected to become familiar to users.
sections.plainLanguage: UCLA-CCN supports standard host names but questions how the proposed names were chosen. It suggests using NIC site codes as a more considered starting point.

sections.title: Completeness and Name Length
sections.content: The comments ask whether host mnemonics should be limited to six characters. They also say that the proposed list showed 20 hosts while a recent BBN list showed 40, and argue that a proposed standard should cover all known hosts at the time.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors question the proposed six-character limit and point out that the list omits many hosts shown in a more recent roster.

sections.title: Specific Name Changes
sections.content:
UCLA-CCN proposes UCLAS7 or UCLANM for host 1 and UCLA91 for host 65, rather than the names in the proposal. It also suggests SRINIC for host 2 because the site was commonly called the NIC rather than SRIARC.

The authors conclude that standards deserve careful consideration rather than preserving what they call historical choices.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives replacement names for UCLA's hosts and SRI's NIC host. These examples support the request to choose names deliberately.
